newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen forces push back opponents.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen forces push back opponents.

text.p: Forces of co-Prime Minister Hun Sen pushed back troops loyal to his deposed rival Prince Norodom Ranariddh in northwest Cambodia on Saturday and Hun Sen said his opponents had failed to organise resistance to him.

Hun Sen's troops, backed by tanks and multiple rocket launchers, forced First Prime Minister Ranariddh's men back along Route Six, west of the northwestern town of Siem Reap, reporters at the scene said.
Hun Sen, whose forces ousted Ranariddh after two days of fighting in Phnom Penh last weekend, said his opponents had tried unsuccessfully to seize several provinces.

"On the first day, people wanted to take Battambang, Siem Reap, Preah Vihear, Kompong Thom to create a state within the state," Hun Sen said at a pagoda-opening ceremony about 25 km (15 miles) from Phnom Penh.
"They could not and they were disappointed because the people didn't want to fight, they don't care about war, they only care about their farming," Hun Sen said.
Officials of Ranariddh's royalist party had vowed to try to capture territory in the provinces to set up a base for their resistance.
In Phnom Penh, a senior member of Ranariddh's royalist party FUNCINPEC said he was ready to replace the prince as first prime minister.

Toan Chay, who broke with Ranariddh in April, said he would agree to be first prime minister if his party chose him. Another leading contender is royalist Co-Defence Minister Tea Chamrath, who also said he would take the job is the party wished.
Hun Sen has denied staging a coup and said he intends to keep the coalition in place by allowing FUNCINPEC to name a new first prime minister. He said he did not want the post himself.

Hun Sen and Ranariddh formed their power-sharing coalition after U.N.-organised elections in May 1993 which Ranariddh won. Never a happy alliance, the coalition began falling apart last year when Ranariddh demanded more power in the provinces.
Toan Chay appealed to his royalist party members not to flee the country and said those who had left had nothing to fear and should come back.
"We (want) to make people gain hope. Do not fear, do not run out of the country," he said. "Come back to align with the government."

Dozens of FUNCINPEC members and royalist sympathisers fled Cambodia after last weekend's fighting and the arrest and subsequent execution of a leading FUNCINPEC official, blamed by Hun Sen for causing the fighting.

In a letter obtained by Reuters on Saturday, London-based Amnesty International expressed serious concerns about the fate of hundreds of soldiers and officials of Ranariddh's party believed to have been captured by Hun Sen's forces.

"We hold grave fears for the safety of the hundreds of FUNCINPEC soldiers and officials believed to be in the custody of your forces," Amnesty secretary-general Pierre Sane said in an open letter to Hun Sen.
Amnesty said it was deeply concerned about the safety of politicians, journalists and activists linked to FUNCINPEC and two smaller parties allied to the royalists.

"We urge you to clarify immediately and publicly the status and welfare of all those being held, provide guarantees for their safety and fair treatment and afford access to them by independent monitors," Sane said. Sane also condemned the reported summary execution of FUNCINPEC officials.
In an apparent reference to the brutality of Cambodia's Khmer Rouge regime, Sane urged Hun Sen to halt alleged human rights abuses.
"You know only too well the spectre of gross human rights violations that haunts Cambodia to this day," he said. More than a million people died in the Maoist Khmer Rouge's 1975-1979 rule.
